claim.precise: Psalm 22:17–18 predicted that Jesus would be stripped, watched and have His clothes divided by lot, fulfilled in Luke 23:34–35.
claim.scope_notes: Luke closely reproduces the garments, lots and watching; the question is whether this is prediction or literary application of a lament.

context.summary: Psalm 22's humiliated sufferer is watched while enemies divide his clothes by lot. Luke places the same actions beside Jesus's crucifixion.

strongest_case.summary: The cluster is unusually close: hostile onlookers, divided garments and casting lots occur together in both texts. All four Gospels preserve the clothing motif, and John explicitly calls it fulfilment of Scripture.
reasoning: The garments, lots and watching appear together in both accounts.
The garments and lots wording is distinctive.
All four Gospels preserve the garments-and-lots motif.

critical_case.summary: The close link shows that Gospel writers interpreted and narrated Jesus's death through Psalm 22. But the psalm is voiced as a current lament, not introduced as a future oracle, and familiarity with it could shape which details were preserved and emphasized.
reasoning: Dependence does not establish independent predictive fulfilment.
The psalm's original grammar describes present distress.

verdict.summary: Luke's scene is a clear and close reuse of Psalm 22. It strongly supports Christian literary application of the psalm, but by itself cannot show that the lament was written as a forecast of Jesus.

objections.objection: Literary dependence and historical fulfilment can coexist.
objections.reason: The verdict says reuse is not independent proof; it does not claim dependence disproves the event or theological fulfilment.

objections.objection: The sequence and precision of the correspondence were overstated.
objections.reason: The strongest case now says the motifs appear together and no longer claims the same order or explicit stripping.

objections.objection: Occurrence in four Gospels is not necessarily independent multiple attestation.
objections.reason: The copy now reports only that all four preserve the motif, without claiming independence.

publication_copy.title: Clothes divided by lot
publication_copy.scripture_excerpt: They divide my garments … and cast lots for my clothing.

website.description: Did Psalm 22 predict what happened to Jesus's clothes?
website.summary: This is one of the closest links between Psalm 22 and the Gospel passion stories.
website.christian_case: The match is detailed: people watch, clothes are divided and lots are cast. John even says the soldiers' action fulfilled this scripture.
website.critical_case: The Gospel connection is exceptionally close. That literary reuse can coexist with a historical event or theological fulfilment, but it cannot by itself prove that the psalm was an advance forecast.
website.verdict_label: A later reading of the psalm
website.verdict: The Gospels deliberately apply Psalm 22 to Jesus. That is strong literary reuse, but not independent proof of a centuries-ahead prediction.

carousel.heading: Did Psalm 22 predict the divided clothes?
carousel.body: The psalm says enemies divide the sufferer’s clothes by lot. Luke describes people doing exactly that to Jesus.

carousel.heading: This is a very close match
carousel.body: The clothes, the lots and the watching crowd appear together. John even calls the soldiers’ action fulfilled Scripture.

carousel.heading: The link is real—but what proves what?
carousel.body: The Gospels use Psalm 22 to explain Jesus’s death. That does not prove the psalm began as a forecast of him.
